OpenCode opencode run --agent <role> --model <provider/model> "<task>"

For more control, use the tools' libraries instead of their command lines: the Claude Agent SDK (@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk or claude-agent-sdk for Python) streams each step and reports the cost of the run; load the project settings (settingSources: ["project"]) so it reads CLAUDE.md and .claude/.

Rules for the worker:

  • one container or VM per task, with write access to that repository only;
  • a Git token that can push branches and open merge requests, never push to main or merge;
  • no production, cluster or registry credentials;
  • record the cost and the outcome on the task, so you notice a role that burns budget.

Good when you need priorities, retries, your own infrastructure or a dashboard of your own. It is your code to maintain: start with the simplest queue that works.

LiteLLM: one gateway for many providers

With OpenCode on several providers, the litellm feature adds infra/litellm/: a LiteLLM gateway (with Postgres and Caddy) that gives each role a virtual key with its own budget, and one place to see costs per role and model. Run it next to your orchestrator, listening only on the local interface, or on a small server for CI. infra/litellm/key-spend.sh shows what each key spent; docker-compose.local.yml runs it on your computer for a trial.

To use it:

  1. Put the gateway's address in opencode.json (provider.litellm.options.baseURL; the setup writes it if you gave the domain) and the providers' keys in infra/litellm/.env, never in a tracked file.
  2. Create one virtual key per role: ./infra/litellm/create-key.sh optimizer deepseek 30 (role, model, monthly budget in dollars).
  3. Give OpenCode the key: locally with /connect, choosing the LiteLLM provider; in CI as a secret in the env of the OpenCode job, with OPENCODE_MODEL set to litellm/<model>.

8. Change and upgrade

Two things change over a project's life: the plugin gets new versions, and your setup changes (another tracker, Codex next to Claude Code, a role back, the move from local to remote). Both go through the same command:

/agent-team:upgrade        (Claude Code)
use the upgrade skill      (Codex, OpenCode)

Change the profile

Tell the upgrade what changes ("move the issues to Linear", "add Codex for the optimizer", "we no longer need the designer") or edit .agent-team/config.json yourself, then run the upgrade. It renders the template for the new profile and shows a plan:

Kind What happens
add a file the new profile includes: added
update a template file you never changed: replaced with the new version
merge changed by both you and the template: three-way merge that keeps your changes
prune a file the profile no longer includes, never changed by you: removed
out-of-profile a file the profile no longer includes, changed by you: kept, you decide
removed-by-you a file you deleted: not added back

Sections follow the same rule: drop team tasks and their section leaves AGENTS.md; add Codex back and its lines return, merged with your edits. Conflicts, if any, are left marked and resolved with you. The upgrade works on a branch and ends with a commit for you to review.

Examples:

You want Profile change What the upgrade does
From local to remote on GitHub "tracker": "github", "features": ["ci-agents", "dispatch"] adds the agent workflows, labels script, issue scripts; then the remote set-up of chapter 6
Codex instead of Claude Code "harnesses": ["codex"] adds .codex/ and .agents/skills/, removes .claude/ and CLAUDE.md if unchanged, switches the CI jobs
Jira instead of GitHub issues "tracker": "jira" plus its settings adds the Jira adapter, removes the GitHub workflows that need GitHub issues
Security back add "security" to roles adds its prompt, agents and scope file

After a tool change, the upgrade lists what that tool needs once: trust and hooks for Codex, new CI secrets and variables.

Without the plugin, python3 scripts/agent-team.py prune removes what left the profile, but only the upgrade can add things back.

Upgrade to a new plugin version

  1. Update the plugin (2. Install).
  2. Run /agent-team:upgrade in the project. It reads the release notes of the versions in between and explains each change, not just the file names.
  3. Review the plan, exclude what you do not want, apply.
  4. Do the steps listed in the release notes' "Upgrade notes": they are the ones a file change cannot do (new secrets, labels, required checks).

Every project stays on the template version it installed until you upgrade it: updating the plugin changes nothing by itself.

How your changes are kept

The setup stores a copy of every installed template file in .agent-team/base/. The upgrade compares three versions of each file: that copy, your file, and the new template file. If only the template changed, your file is replaced; if only you changed it, nothing happens; if both changed, git merge-file merges them and marks the lines it cannot decide.

README.md, docs/design-decisions.md (the decision log), .mcp.json (the MCP servers the agents may use) and docs/roles/security-scope.txt are yours after setup: they are never upgraded (3. What you get).

A project set up by hand

A project copied from the template without the plugin, or set up before the plugin existed, has no .agent-team/base/. The first upgrade proposes a profile from what the project has, then compares each file that differs with you and records the result; later upgrades are automatic. Without Claude Code, run it from a clone:

python3 ~/agent-team/scripts/template_sync.py status --template ~/agent-team/template --project .
python3 ~/agent-team/scripts/template_sync.py apply  --template ~/agent-team/template --project .

9. Reference

Skills

Plugin skill Template skill What it does
setup installs and configures the template; first time only; --to-issues also creates the issues
design-studio /design-studio design session for the project, a feature or a whole milestone (--milestone M0), writes the specs; --to-issues goes on to the issues and the split
create-issues milestones and issues from the roadmap and the ready specs; turns "Design:" issues into features and tasks
split-issue one or several issues (or a milestone) into one task per role, after your approval of each

/handoff a short note so a fresh session continues the work

/document has the writer agent write or update the software documentation in docs/software/

Claude can propose next, design-studio, create-issues, split-issue and dispatch by itself; each shows its plan and asks before changing anything. setup and upgrade run only when you type them.

Plugin skills come with the plugin (or the clone of the repository, for Codex and OpenCode) and work in every project: in Claude Code they are /agent-team:<name>; in Codex and OpenCode ask for them by name. Template skills are copied into each project (.claude/skills/, .agents/skills/), so they work for anyone who opens the project, with or without the plugin. design-studio is both: the two run the same procedure, docs/roles/design-studio.md; use the plugin's when you have it, since only it has --to-issues.

Scripts

Command What it does
python3 scripts/agent-team.py profile the profile, and what is outside it
python3 scripts/agent-team.py prune [--dry-run] removes files and sections outside the profile
python3 scripts/tracker.py check \| config \| list \| show N the tracker: connection, settings, open issues, one issue
python3 scripts/create-issues.py [--dry-run] [--team] [--migrate] milestones and issues; a "Design:" issue whose spec is ready becomes the task (one row) or the feature with the tasks as sub-issues; --migrate moves old "M0 · ..." parent issues to milestones
python3 scripts/split-issue.py check \| propose \| create the split of one issue: validate a plan, post it, create it; "depends_on": ["12:api"] waits for a task of issue 12's plan, which must be created first

scripts/git-hooks/spec-sync.sh feature spec-sync, local: Git hook (post-merge, post-commit) that runs create-issues after a spec change on the main branch
./scripts/create-labels.sh GitHub labels
./scripts/install-skills.sh, ./scripts/check-skills.sh recommended skills for your stack, and a check that the agents find them

.agent-team/config.json, every key optional:

Key Meaning

Environment variables AGENT_TEAM_TRACKER, AGENT_TEAM_STARTER and AGENT_TEAM_START_COMMAND override the file. Secrets only in the environment: JIRA_EMAIL + JIRA_API_TOKEN or JIRA_PAT, LINEAR_API_KEY, REDMINE_API_KEY.

Name Where Used by
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY or CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN GitHub secret, GitLab variable Claude Code jobs
OPENAI_API_KEY secret / variable Codex jobs
CODEX_MODEL GitHub variable Codex model (empty: Codex's default)
AGENT_PR_TOKEN GitHub secret Codex pull requests that start the CI
OPENCODE_MODEL, provider keys variable, secrets OpenCode jobs
AGENT_RUNNERS, AGENT_DEFAULT_RUNNER GitHub variables which tool runs which role
AGENT_AUTODISPATCH, AGENT_DISPATCH_TOKEN GitHub variable, secret dispatch at every merge
AGENT_DISPATCH_PER_ROLE, AGENT_DISPATCH_MAX GitHub variables its limits (1 and 3)
GITLAB_ACCESS_TOKEN GitLab variable splits; spec-sync; Codex and OpenCode merge requests
JIRA_EMAIL + JIRA_API_TOKEN or JIRA_PAT, LINEAR_API_KEY, REDMINE_API_KEY GitHub secrets, GitLab variables spec-sync and dispatch in CI with those trackers
AI_FLOW_*, TASK_ID, SPLIT_* GitLab pipeline variables starting a job (6. Scenario: remote)

Where the tools find things

Claude Code Codex OpenCode
Project rules CLAUDE.md → AGENTS.md AGENTS.md AGENTS.md
Roles .claude/agents/*.md .codex/agents/*.toml .opencode/agents/*.md
Skills .claude/skills/ .agents/skills/ .claude/skills/ or .agents/skills/
Forbidden commands .claude/settings.json .codex/rules/agent-team.rules permission in opencode.json and agents
Hooks .claude/settings.json → scripts/hooks/ .codex/hooks.json → scripts/hooks/ none
Settings .claude/settings.json .codex/config.toml opencode.json

What a run costs

Agent team adds no fees: you pay the model provider (an API key, billed per token) or use your subscription's quota, plus CI minutes for runs in CI. A run's cost depends on the model, the size of the task and of the code it reads, so the template bounds each run instead:

Run Limit
a task, Claude Code on GitHub 40 turns, 60 minutes
a team task, GitHub 100 turns, 120 minutes
a task, Claude Code on GitLab 30 turns
an @claude mention, an ai-review review 15 turns each
Codex or OpenCode jobs 60 minutes

A turn is one model response, with its tool calls. Every run compacts its context at 200,000 tokens. To see what runs actually cost, look at your provider's usage page after a few tasks; with the custom orchestrator, the Claude Agent SDK reports the cost of each run, and LiteLLM the spend per role. Start with low dispatch limits (one task per role, three in total) and raise them once you know your numbers.

Token costs

What every agent reads on every turn costs on every request: AGENTS.md (about 1,200 tokens after setup), CLAUDE.md, the descriptions of the agents and skills of the tool in use, and the tools of active MCP servers. Role prompts, specs and docs/agents/ cost only when an agent opens them. Files of other tools, trackers and workflows cost nothing unless an agent searches or opens them: the profile removes them anyway, so no agent stumbles on instructions for tools you do not have.

To keep costs down: one task per session, handoff notes instead of long sessions, MCP servers only on the agents that need them, and few skills per role.

This manual

For people who change the manual itself, in the plugin's repository; nothing to do in your projects. The manual is written in Markdown, one file per chapter in docs/manual/. docs/manual.html is generated from those files and never edited by hand:

pip install markdown==3.11.2
python3 scripts/build_manual.py           # regenerate docs/manual.html
python3 scripts/build_manual.py --check   # fails if the HTML is not built from the current Markdown

The HTML records a hash of the Markdown it was built from; --check compares it with the files, and the repository's CI runs it on every pull request. To check before every commit: git config core.hooksPath .githooks.
